messages.body_plain:
If you have specific models in mind that you want to fit to each group, you can fit them as a multiple-group model.  The two groups can have different factor structures by imposing the appropriate constraints.  For example, if you think x4 measures visual in the first group but not the second, you just fix the second group's loading to zero, while estimating it in the first group:

> visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + c(NA, 0)*x4

When you fit the two hypothesized models simultaneously as a multiple-group model, the chi-squared fit statistic will tell you whether the model-implied covariance matrices differ statistically from the observed covariance matrices.  If so, you could consult the modification indices in conjunction with standardized expected parameter changes (EPCs) to see which constrained parameters the data don't seem to corroborate.

If you want to compare models (e.g., a model with equal factor structure across groups, and a model with different factor structure across groups), then you have 2 possibilities: (a) If they are nested models, then a chi-squared difference test could tell you whether the simpler model fits significantly better than the model with more parameters.  (b)  If the models are not nested, you can compare them using AIC (or BIC).  See the semTools function "net()" for a test of whether models are nested/equivalent.

If you want to test whether specific parameters are higher/lower in one group than the other, then you can also use the chi-squared difference test.  Fit a model where the same factor loading is freely estimated in both groups, then fit another model where you constrain that parameter to equality across groups (by giving it the same label):
Model 1: visual =~ x1 + c(a, b)*x2 + x3
Model 2: visual =~ x1 + c(a, a)*x2 + x3
If the change in chi-squared indicates significantly better fit for Model 1, then you can conclude that the parameters differ across groups (so one is higher than the other, for reasons other than sampling fluctuation).

Bear in mind that SEM requires large sample sizes (e.g., minimum 100 per group for a model this size, but probably twice that for parameter estimates with any decent precision -- check your SEs to judge the quality of the estimates).  So if you have adequate Ns, you might have enough power to detect trivial differences, so you could also refer to the approximate fit using CFI, RMSEA, etc.

There is a lot of literature available about SEM model fit -- try searching issues of the SEM journal <http://www.tandfonline.com/toc/hsem20/current#.Ve1GRBGeDRY> and the archives of the SEMNET list-serv <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>.  Since your questions are as much about SEM in general as about specific software issues, you could probably find help from a wider and more diverse audience of researchers by posting your problem there.

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical models with varying number of indicator variables for the FOLVs
messages.body_plain:
> I wonder whether it's possible to construct hierarchical models when the number of indicator variables for each FOLV varies.

There is no assumption about latent variables having the same number of indicators.  Special constraints are needed when you have only 1 or 2 indicators of a factor, but all latent variables in your model (first- or second-order) can have different numbers of indicators.

> Is such a model statistically feasible?

Only if you have a very large sample size, so that your model converges and the parameter estimates are estimated with any decent amount of precision.  I wouldn't feel comfortable fitting a model with 19 FOLVs using any less that N = 2000 on the small side (I base that on intuition and previous experience, with no data to support that number -- there is free literature available on simulation-based power analyses using Mplus).

> Perhaps also worth noting that the data is nearly all in Likert-type scales, or dichotomous.

That might be a problem for LVs with only 1 indicator (I don't think that can be identified).

>  I have attached a sketch of the first 7 FOLVS - the page would be a lot wider if I was sketch the whole thing.  Also each SOLV is hypothesised to influence each other (is this possible when specifying the relationship between FOLVs?

Yes.  The second-order "factor loadings" are in the Beta matrix, with all the  other latent-variable regression coefficients.  So there is no statistical distinction between a second-order factor loading and a latent regression slope, just in how you interpret them (although that is how you interpret loadings -- as slopes).

Since this is a general SEM question rather than a lavaan issue, it would be more appropriate to post this on SEMNET.  That might also be advantageous for you, as it has been around longer and has a larger audience of people who could help.

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

Terry

I'm going to guess this is an R issue (if it's an issue at all), not a Lavaan issue.

If you use the pchisq() function, with 0 df, you always get a p-value of 0.

> pchisq(3.84, 0, lower.tail=FALSE)
[1] 0

This is what Lavaan is doing.

So then we need to know why the df are the same. I imagine that it's something in the defaults. You don't say which function you used (lavaan() or sem(), but they have slightly different defaults - in your first model some default parameters were added. In the second, because some things have changed, they were not added.

For example:
y1 ~ x1 + x2
y2 ~ y1

Will (I believe) correlate x1 and x2.  Add an additional path:
x1 ~ y2
And x1 and x2 will no longer correlate by default. The model is different (and so the model fit will be different) but the df will be the same.

Check the parameters to see what has changed.

Jeremy

It means you can't use the asterisk operator to automatically calculate product terms, like you can in lm() and glm().  And there is no support for latent moderated structural equations (but the semTools package has functions to support latent interactions using product indicators).

Yes, if State and Poverty are observed variables in your model, you need to add the product term StPov to your data.frame in order to include it in your model.

messages.body_plain:
> How can I conduct a moderation analysis for them in lavaan? I tried using the measurement invariance cat function, but get too many errors

Including your R script (and perhaps enough data to reproduce the error) would be the first step toward getting help with it.  If you are testing measurement invariance, you are fitting CFAs (all latent variables are "exogenous" in the sense of not having any predictors).  So I imagine that you are using the ordinal "moderator" as a grouping variable, and testing invariance across those groups?

> I couldn't understand his script, he appeared to make modifications in models rather than the formula syntax.

The formula syntax is where you specify your model(s), so I am not sure what you mean.

> First question:
> Can anyone tell me a simple manual way to test measurement invariance in lavaan, one that's not too particular but enough to determine if I can compare means .

Establishing strong invariance as illustrated in those scripts, or using the measurementInvarianceCat() function -- both were designed to help with this.  Without seeing your own attempt to fit those models, it is impossible to tell what is going wrong.

> Second question: this may sound stupid but kindly also tell me how to compare means for moderation in lavaan and interpret it?

This sounds like you are conflating 2 concepts.  You can compare the unconditional/grand means of exogenous latent variables (i.e., all variables in a CFA) across groups by establishing strong invariance, then constraining latent means to equality to see if the model fit is significantly worse.

If you are testing moderation, that implies you are running a regression.  So your question isn't about whether the latent means differ across groups, but about whether the regression path(s) differ(s) across groups (e.g., does the effect of X on Y depend on which level of M your are talking about?).  In the case of a latent regression (full structural) model, you can still compare latent means of exogenous latent variables across groups, but in the case of endogenous latent variables, you don't estimate an unconditional mean.  Rather, you estimate an intercept, which is a conditional mean (the mean of the outcome conditioned on the predictor(s) being held constant at 0).  You can test group-differences in intercepts (or any other conditional mean) if there are particular levels of X for which you have a theoretical reason to test mean-differences in Y -- but typically those aren't of substantive interest.  Rather, moderation is a question of whether an effect (regression path) differs across levels of a moderator.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
To start, in the first output, note that the intercepts / means for er, ma, g1, he and g are all fixed (to 0).  The second syntax appears to be trying to freely estimate these parameters in both groups.  That would account for a difference of 10 DF between the two outputs, which is the difference in the two results.  For the meanstructure part of the model, the only information you have, to estimate parameters from, is the means of the observed variables.  With two groups and 7 observed variables, you cannot estimate more than 14 meanstructure parameters.  Your second syntax will have to impose more constraints.  The first syntax constrains these parameters to 0 but freely estimates observed variable means / intercepts (plus the intercept for g1) in both groups.  If you want to estimate factor means / intercepts in one group, you will need to constrain the factor means / intercepts in the other group (say, to 0) and also constrain observed variable intercepts to equality across groups.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject_clean: different ML estimatest between Lavaan & Mplus
messages.body_plain:
On 09/20/2015 12:09 AM, Phil Wood wrote:
> I'm somewhat puzzled by the following. Both Lavaan and Mplus converge,
> but I'm puzzled that the LL is different and that the paramter estimates
> are so different. The example I show here is 300 observations, six
> variables and no missing data.
> I've attached the lavaan program (factormeanshift.R), the Mplus program
> (fmshift2.inp) and the data (sixtimegrowth.txt). Any ideas?

Blame the optimizer. Usually, the optimizer used by lavaan (nlminb)
performs really well. But every now and then, it may get stuck in a
local optimum (and think it converged). The flatter the parameter space,
the more likely this is to happen.

In this particular example, Mplus and Onyx do find a better solution. In
other examples, lavaan finds the better solution. But in my experience,
discrepancies like these mostly happen for models that are very
mis-specified (note that the X^2 value is a factor 80-90 larger than the
degrees of freedom).

It would appear that the following trick helps:

fit <- sem(FactorMeanShift.model, data = curvedata,
control=list(init_nelder_mead=TRUE), verbose = TRUE)

(this forces a number of 'Nelder-Mead' iterations before the
quasi-newton optimizer kicks in). Unfortunately, in almost all but a few
cases, this does not help at all.

In lavaan 0.6, I will add support for external optimizers if they are
available (eg package nloptr), and if I can find an optimizer that
consistently performs better than nlminb(), I will make the switch.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
The link is showing you how to test invariance, which is done using CFAs.  So there are no latent regression slopes in those models, but you need to establish weak invariance to check whether latent regressions can even be compared across groups.  AFTER establishing at least weak invariance, then you can change the CFA to a structural model (replacing latent covariances with latent regression slopes).  Testing latent slopes for across-group differences follows the same logic as testing factor loadings for across-group differences, and uses the same syntax rules:
Fit a model without any constraints on the latent regression slope(s)
Fit a model with constraints across groups by giving them the same label, for example (in a 3-group model):  Factor2 ~ c(beta21, beta21, beta21)*Factor1
Use the anova() method to calculate a chi-squared-difference test.  If it is significant, the equality constraints are not tenable, so you can conclude there is moderation (slopes differ across groups).  If you are interested in specific pairwise comparisons, you can constrain 2 slopes at a time: Factor2 ~ c(beta21, beta21, beta21_g3)*Factor1

Terry

messages.subject: Re: computing Rasch values within SEM using lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: computing Rasch values within SEM using lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
On 09/20/2015 04:18 PM, isomitzi wrote:
> i have a smallish data set (700 cases) and 40 items on a likert scale
> (1-5). i would like to run SEM on the items but would like the items to
> be on a Rasch scale.

Strictly speaking, Rasch only deals with binary items. For ordinal
items, a popular method is the graded response model. Instead of a
single 'difficulty' parameter, you will get a set of 4 thresholds per
item. In addition, by default, lavaan will allow the factor loadings
(which can be converted to discrimination parameters) to be different
for each item. In the spirit of Rasch, you may want to force them to be
equal for all items.

> is there a way to do it all in Lavaan?
>
> let's say i have 8 items : I1-I8 which should represent 2 latent
> constructs (L1 and L2) that are first order factors and F1 which is a
> second level factor:
>
> L1=~ I1+I2+I3+I4
> L2=~ I5+I6+I7+I8
> F1=~ L1+L2 (not sure if i should use =~ or just ~)

The second order factor is not identified without further restrictions.
If you are using std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, you should constrain one factor loading
to 1.0:

model <- '
L1 =~ I1 + I2 + I3 + I4
L2 =~ I5 + I6 + I7 + I8
F1 =~ 1*L1 + L2
'

fit <- cfa(model, data = ..., std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, ordered = paste0("I",1:8))

If I1-I8 are ordinal, this will correspond with the graded response model.

If you wish to constrain the factor loadings to be equal (within each
latent variable), you need to use labels. Same labels imply same
parameter values:

model <- '
L1=~ a*I1 + a*I2 + a*I3 + a*I4
L2=~ b*I5 + b*I6 + b*I7 + b*I8
F1=~ 1*L1+L2
'

And of course, you can add regressions to this model...

Yves.

Unless std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE was used to begin with, this is generally not true.
The p-values of unstandardized (say, covariance) parameters are not the
same as the p-values of the corresponding standardized (here,
correlation) parameters. The sampling distributions are different. In
fact, it can happen that the p-value for the covariance is significant,
while the p-value for the correlation is not.

The standardizedSolution() output will give p-values for standardized
parameters.

Yves.

Dear lavaan users,

I have rolled up a 'release candidate' for lavaan 0.5-19. To install
this version, type in R:

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")

and it should be version 0.5-18.887 (or higher).

Can you give it a try and check if it doesn't break anything? If all
goes well, I hope to upload this version to CRAN by the end of the week.

This is mainly a maintenance update, with only a few new features:

- a new print function for the 'parameter estimates' section of the
summary() output; the 'section' headers are now repeated, and you can
adjust the number of digits after the decimal point, as in

summary(fit, nd = 5)

- new function lavScoreTest() to get univariate and multivariate score
tests (aka Lagrange Multiplier Tests); see ?lavScoreTest for more
information

Yves.

> > what does it mean that "Interaction terms are currently not supported" in the special growth() function of lavaan?

> It means you can't use the asterisk operator to automatically calculate product terms, like you can in lm() and glm().  And there is no support for latent moderated structural equations (but the semTools package has functions to support latent interactions using product indicators).
